# Local ordinary depth stability in every dimension

This theorem concerns ordinary continuous volume and maximum depth.
It does not assert OC or an integer-fiber allocation principle.

Let d>=2, m=d+1, and define

    Gamma=(d/m)^d,
    c=[1-d^(1-d)]/[(d-1)^2(d+1)]>0.                (1)

There is a dimension-only epsilon_d>0 such that every convex body K
which is within epsilon_d of a simplex in an affine Hausdorff-infinity
frame has a minimum-volume enclosing simplex S satisfying

    D(K)-Gamma >=(Gamma*c/4)(1-|K|/|S|).           (2)

Here D(K) is the maximum, over y in K, of the fraction of ordinary
d-volume in the least closed halfspace containing y. The proof below
constructs one actual interior point that gives (2). In particular,
for normalized uniform measures and cap distance defined as supremum
over all closed halfspaces,

    dist_cap(mu_K,mu_S)<=TV(mu_K,mu_S)
       =1-|K|/|S| <=4[D(K)-Gamma]/(Gamma*c).        (3)

The radius can be defined from explicit geometric constants and a
strict compact normal gap of the standard simplex, as detailed below.
There is no approximation by a fixed-facet or smooth family, and no
unquantified relative remainder is used.

## 1. Dependencies and the stronger relative formulation

We use three proved auxiliary results, with their roles stated exactly.

1. The critical simplex martingale and its sharp quantitative extension
   in `candidate c6aadce19d219a98` and
   `candidate 81d65baa0f0a1024`. On a facet F
   with d barycentric coordinates, if f>=0 is continuous convex and
   f(g_F)=0, the latter gives

       int_F N f <=m Gamma(1-c) int_F f,           (4)
       N(z)=#{i:lambda_i(z)>=1/m}.

   All integrals here and below on a facet use normalized facet volume.
   One coordinate of its ambient simplex barycentrics is identically
   zero and does not enter N. Equation (4) follows by applying the
   proved inequality to -f. It holds for ALL such convex functions,
   including ones concentrated near lower-dimensional boundary faces.

2. The attained enclosing-simplex theorem in
   `candidate 783495094e97ee67`.
   Every convex body has a minimum-volume enclosing simplex; every
   facet centroid of every minimizer belongs to the body. If K is
   within epsilon of the standard d-simplex T, with epsilon sufficiently
   small, its minimizing simplex has vertices corresponding to those
   of T within 8d^3 epsilon. The source proves this by bounded vertex
   tuples, an explicit feasible facet tilt, and cone volume bounds.

3. The ordinary simplex cap minimum at its centroid is Gamma and its
   only minimizing normals are the d+1 apex-side facet-parallel ones.
   The equality classification is proved in
   `candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`; its compact
   all-normal consequence and exact vertex-cap formula are restated
   in Section2 of `candidate 3795aff5f3322d52`.

The new theorem proved first is stronger than a Hausdorff formulation:
there is delta_d>0 such that (2) holds whenever

    (1-delta)S+delta g_S subset K subset S,
    0<=delta<=delta_d,
    every facet centroid of S belongs to K.        (5)

All ordinary affine transformations preserve this hypothesis, depth,
and volume ratios. We may use standard simplex coordinates for S.
The case delta=0 is immediate, so take delta>0 below.

## 2. Uniform weighted strip estimate on a simplex facet

We include an elementary proof to make the all-normal estimate explicit.
On a k-dimensional simplex F, let f>=0 be continuous convex. For a
barycentric coordinate t, conditional averaging over the other
coordinates gives

    A(t)=int f(t,(1-t)w) dmu_(k-1)(w),
    M=int_0^1 k(1-t)^(k-1) A(t) dt=int_F f.        (6)

The function A is convex and nonnegative, since for each fixed w its
argument is affine in t. For k=1 the opposite simplex is a point,
and the same formula holds with density1. Fix b in(0,1), and put

    r=(1/4)min{b,(1-b)/k}.

For |t-b|<=r, the interval [t-r,t+r] is in(0,1). Jensen and positivity
give A(t)<= (1/(2r))int_(t-r)^(t+r) A(s) ds. Hence

    k(1-t)^(k-1) A(t)
      <=(M/(2r))*[(1-t)/(1-t-r)]^(k-1) <=M/r.     (7)

For the last bound set x=r/(1-t). Since t<=b+r and
r<=(1-b)/(4k), one has x<=1/(4k-1). Bernoulli gives
(1-x)^(k-1)>=1-(k-1)/(4k-1)>1/2. This proves (7), including k=1.
Integration over |t-b|<=eta<=r gives

    int_{|t-b|<=eta} f <=(2eta/r) int_F f.          (8)

For the facets in (5), k=d-1 and b=1/m, so

    r=1/(4m),  C=2/r=8m,
    int_{|lambda_i-b|<=eta} f <=C eta int_F f.     (9)

This bound is uniform in f. In particular it assumes no bound on
sup f divided by its integral. On the opposite facet F_i, lambda_i
is identically zero; the strip is empty for eta<b.

## 3. Radial gauge and exact missing-volume disintegration

Let g=g_S, and let rho be the Minkowski gauge of K-g, evaluated on
vectors relative to g. Since g is interior to K by (5), this gauge
is finite, continuous, nonnegative, and convex. Explicitly convexity
follows from the inclusion of convex combinations in K: if v in a(K-g)
and w in b(K-g), then v+w is in (a+b)(K-g); combine this subadditivity
with positive homogeneity and continuity. Along a ray to a facet point
z in F_j, the K boundary is at

    g+R(z)(z-g), R(z)=1/rho(z-g).

Put f_j(z)=rho(z-g)-1 and w_j(z)=1-rho(z-g)^(-d). Since K subset S
and contains the inner simplex in (5),

    0<=f_j<=delta/(1-delta),
    1-delta<=R<=1,
    d(1-delta)^d f_j<=w_j<=d f_j.                 (10)

For (10), when rho>1 the exact quotient is
w_j/f_j=sum_(a=1)^d rho^(-a); at rho=1 both sides vanish and the
limit is d. Each f_j is convex on its facet and vanishes at its
facet centroid: that point is in K and on the S boundary, forcing
its gauge to equal1. Thus (4) applies.

The d+1 pyramids conv(g,F_j) partition S up to null boundaries and
have equal volume |S|/m. In each, uniform volume disintegrates into
uniform z on F_j and radial density d r^(d-1) on0<=r<=1. Therefore,
with tau=1-|K|/|S|,

    tau=(1/m)sum_j int_Fj w_j.                    (11)

Let C_i={lambda_i>=b} be the canonical centroid cap, and let

    R_i=|(S\K) intersect C_i|/|S|.

Along a ray, lambda_i(g+r(z-g))-b=r(lambda_i(z)-b), so canonical
cap membership is constant except at the null center. Thus

    sum_i R_i=(1/m)sum_j int_Fj N(z) w_j(z)
      <=m Gamma(1-c)(1-delta)^(-d) tau.            (12)

The first inequality uses w_j<=d f_j, (4), and then the other side
of (10) with (11). This is the exact place where facet-centroid
contact and the new functional inequality improve the loss budget.

## 4. All nearby halfspaces have a uniform relative loss error

Suppose a halfspace H has affine defining margin phi, with H={phi>=0},
and on S

    |phi(x)-(lambda_i(x)-b)|<=eta.                (13)

If a missing point x is in H but not in C_i, then
|lambda_i(x)-b|<=eta. On a missing ray r>=R(z)>=1-delta; hence its
facet endpoint obeys

    |lambda_i(z)-b|<=eta/(1-delta).               (14)

If eta/(1-delta)<=1/(4m), (9)-(11) and (10) give

    |(S\K) intersect H|/|S|
      <= R_i+C eta(1-delta)^(-d-1) tau.            (15)

Indeed the extra mass is bounded by (1/m)sum_j int_strip w_j;
replace w_j by d f_j, use (9) with width eta/(1-delta), and convert
back using (10). The facet with constant coordinate zero adds nothing.
This bound treats EVERY halfspace satisfying (13), irrespective of
how its normal, its threshold, or the missing set varies. Closed
boundary hyperplanes have zero ordinary d-volume. No ratio of a
supremum to missing volume has entered the proof.

Choose once and for all

    eta=min{1/(8m), Gamma*c/[4*C*2^(d+1)]},
    E=C eta 2^(d+1)<=Gamma*c/4.                   (16)

For delta<=1/2, the hypotheses of (15) hold and its extra term is
at most E tau. Define the simultaneous bounds

    L_i=min{tau, R_i+E tau}, Lbar=(1/m)sum_i L_i. (17)

They bound all losses in the respective halfspace neighborhoods and
satisfy0<=L_i<=tau. If also delta<=c/(4d), then Bernoulli gives
(1-delta)^d>=1-c/4. Since
(1-c)/(1-c/4)<=1-3c/4, equations (12), (16), (17) imply

    sum_i L_i<=m Gamma(1-c/2)tau,
    Lbar<=Gamma(1-c/2)tau.                        (18)

## 5. Compact all-normal localization and one interior point

For a unit normal u and a point y in S, the S cap volume through y
is jointly continuous in (u,y): indicators converge except on the
limiting hyperplane, which has zero d-volume. At g the only minimizing
normals are the m canonical ones, by dependency3.

Choose small disjoint open neighborhoods U_i of those unit normals.
They and a number chi>0 may be chosen so that for every point with
|lambda_j(y)-b|<=chi and every u in U_i, the margin

    phi_(u,y)(x)=|grad lambda_i| u dot(x-y)

satisfies (13) uniformly on S. At the canonical unit normal and y=g
it is exactly lambda_i(x)-b, so this follows from continuity after
shrinking both neighborhoods and chi. The neighborhoods can also be
chosen so that the included side has exactly vertex i, since eta<b
and the vertex margins have strict signs. On the compact complement
of their union, the cap fraction at g has minimum Gamma+rho_0 for
some rho_0>0. Shrink chi again so that every such cap at the indicated
points has fraction at least Gamma+rho_0/2. These choices depend only
on d and the explicit eta, and define positive constants chi,rho_0.

Now choose y by its barycentric coordinates

    lambda_i(y)=b+(Lbar-L_i)/(m Gamma).            (19)

They sum to one and differ from b by at most tau/(m Gamma). If
tau<=Gamma/2 and delta<=1/4, every coordinate is at least b/2,
strictly above delta/m. Thus y is in the interior of the inner
simplex in (5), and hence in int K. If tau<=m Gamma chi it also
belongs to the cap-localization neighborhood.

For a cap through y isolating vertex i, the usual intercept formula
and AM-GM give the exact lower bound

    |S intersect H|/|S|>=d^d product_(j!=i) lambda_j(y). (20)

To verify it, express the cap as sum_(j!=i) a_j lambda_j<=1, where
a_j>1 and sum a_j lambda_j(y)=1. Its fraction is product a_j^(-1),
and AM-GM on the d summands gives (20).

Write delta_i=lambda_i(y)-b. For tau<=Gamma, expansion of the product
and |m delta_i|<=tau/Gamma show

    d^d product_(j!=i)lambda_j(y)
      >=Gamma-m Gamma delta_i-B tau^2,
    B=2^d/Gamma.                                 (21)

Indeed all terms of degree at least2 have absolute sum at most
Gamma*sum_(k=2)^d binom(d,k)(tau/Gamma)^k<=B tau^2. Equations
(15)-(19) therefore give every through-y cap with u in U_i the
actual K fraction, measured relative to |S|, at least

    Gamma-Lbar-B tau^2
      >=Gamma-Gamma(1-c/2)tau-B tau^2.             (22)

For all other normals the S fraction is at least Gamma+rho_0/2.
Removing at most tau<=rho_0/4 leaves more than Gamma, so (22) holds
there too. Every containing halfspace can be tightened parallel to
itself through y; measure monotonicity proves (22) for those as well.

If in addition tau<=Gamma*c/(4B), division by |K|/|S|=1-tau yields

    depth_K(y)-Gamma
      >=[Gamma*c*tau/2-B tau^2]/(1-tau)
      >=Gamma*c*tau/4.                            (23)

This constructs the single actual point that proves (2), for every
closed halfspace and every orientation.

For definiteness set

    tau_*=min{Gamma/2,m Gamma chi,rho_0/4,Gamma*c/(4B)},
    delta_d=min{1/4,c/(4d),tau_*/d}.              (24)

Because (5) gives tau<=1-(1-delta)^d<=d delta, these constants
verify all preceding restrictions simultaneously. If tau=0, nested
compact convex bodies with interior and equal volume coincide, so
K=S; its centroid gives equality. This proves the relative theorem.

## 6. Every body sufficiently near a simplex satisfies the hypotheses

Normalize the reference simplex to T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d). Let
L=8(d+1)^3, and take

    epsilon_d=min{1/[64(d+1)^3],
                       delta_d/[d(d+1)(L+1)]}.   (25)

Let dist_H,infinity(K,T)<=epsilon_d, and choose an attained minimum
enclosing simplex S. Dependency2 labels its vertices within L epsilon_d
of those of T, and hence its centroid g_S within that amount of g_T.
Its Hausdorff distance from T is bounded the same way. The infinity
ball of radius1/[d(d+1)] around g_T is contained in T, so for every
linear functional u,

    h_T(u)-u dot g_T>=|u|_1/[d(d+1)].

Support-function comparisons consequently give

    h_((1-delta_d)S+delta_d g_S)(u)
      <=h_T(u)-delta_d |u|_1/[d(d+1)]
                                      +L epsilon_d |u|_1
      <=h_T(u)-epsilon_d |u|_1 <=h_K(u).           (26)

Thus the inner simplex is contained in K. All facet centroids of S
belong to K by the same dependency. The relative theorem applies,
giving (2)-(3). Ordinary affine invariance transports the chosen S
and the actual point y back to the original coordinates.

Dimension1 is separate: every convex body is an interval, its minimum
enclosing simplex is itself, and its midpoint has depth1/2. There is
no use of the undefined d=1 expression in (1). All bodies in this
theorem have positive ordinary d-volume; no claim about lower-dimensional
mixed fibers follows from this ordinary affine normalization.
